results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
You need to keep tax‐related records for the length of time the IRS could still need them to enforce tax laws or the taxpayer can still amend the return. The IRS publications say:

* “You must keep your records as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code. Generally, this means you must keep records that support an item of income or deduction on a return until the period of limitations for that return runs out.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

* “Employment taxes. If you have employees, you must keep all employment tax records for at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

* “Keep records relating to property until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition. You must keep these records to figure any depreciation, amortization, or depletion deduction, and to figure your basis for computing gain or loss when you sell or otherwise dispose of the property.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

* “When your records are no longer needed for tax purposes, do not discard them until you check to see if you have to keep them longer for other purposes. For example, your insurance company or creditors may require you to keep them longer than the IRS does.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

These passages provide the specific retention periods that the IRS requires for tax records.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

results.question: why do i need to keep business records
results.answer:
Because the documents show, you must keep business records for several concrete reasons:

* **To support the amounts on your tax return.**  
  “You need good records to prepare your tax returns. These records must support the income, expenses, and credits you report.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

* **To satisfy the IRS’s requirement to keep records for the period of limitations.**  
  “You must keep your records as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code … you must keep records that support an item of income or deduction on a return until the period of limitations for that return runs out.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

* **To provide documentation in case the IRS inspects your returns.**  
  “You must keep your business records available at all times for inspection by the IRS. If the IRS examines any of your tax returns, you may be asked to explain the items reported. A complete set of records will speed up the examination.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

* **To monitor the progress of your business.**  
  “Good records will help you do the following. Monitor the progress of your business….” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

* **To prepare accurate financial statements.**  
  “Good records to prepare accurate financial statements. These statements can help you….” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

* **To keep track of deductible expenses and other specific records.**  
  “You need to keep supporting documents, ... It is important to keep these documents because they support the entries in your books and on your tax return.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

In short, the documents say that business records are required to prove tax figures, keep the IRS satisfied, meet statutory retention periods, aid in business management, and produce financial statements.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 11)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)
2. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

results.question: what accounting method should i use
results.answer:
You choose an accounting method when you file your first business tax return (Schedule C, Form 1040).  The method you pick must fit your business activities and, once it’s chosen, you must keep it the same unless you get IRS approval to change it【irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 14】.

**Available methods**

* **Cash method** – report income when you receive it and expenses when you pay them.  Most sole‑propietors who have no inventory use this method because it’s simpler【irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 16】.  
* **Accrual method** – report income when you earn it and expenses when you incur them, even if you haven’t yet received or paid cash.  If your business needs to keep inventory, you must use an accrual method for purchases and sales【irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 16】.  
* **Special methods** – for specific items of income or expense (e.g., depreciation, bad debts).  
* **Combination method** – a mix of cash, accrual, and special methods, provided it consistently shows your income and clearly separates inventory treatment if applicable【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 5】.

**When to use each**

* If you **don’t keep inventory** (or can treat inventory as non‑incidental material or supplies), you may choose the **cash method**.  
* If you **do keep inventory**, you must **use the accrual method** for inventory purchases and sales, though you may still use cash for other items.  

So, start by determining whether your business holds inventory. If it does, use the accrual method for inventory; otherwise, the cash method is usually appropriate. If you later want to change the method, you must file Form 1128 or Form 3115 and obtain IRS approval【irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 14】【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 5】.

results.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
results.answer:
To check your workplace for hazards you should use **routine self‑inspections** and the **self‑inspection checklists** that the handbook provides.

1. **Perform a self‑inspection**  
   The handbook says:  
   *“Workplace Self‑Inspection  
   An effective way to identify workplace hazards is for knowledgeable and experienced workers to conduct routine safety and health inspections (i. e. , self‑inspections). The only way to know if potential hazards exist and if they are under control is to assess work processes directly.”*  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

2. **Follow the three‑step inspection process** – identify, control, and monitor – as listed in the handbook:  
   *“• identify hazards,  
   • control identified hazards,  
   • monitor and evaluate hazard controls to verify that they continue to be effective.”*  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

3. **Use the self‑inspection checklists** to structure your review. The handbook explains:  
   *“Self‑Inspection Checklists  
   The checklists in the handbook are intended for general industry workplaces, but not for construction or maritime industries. They are a starting point for identifying workplace hazards. The checklists can give you some indication of where to begin taking action to make your business safer and more healthful for your workers.”*  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

4. **Integrate inspections with a safety and health program**. As part of the recommended practices, hazard identification and assessment is one of the seven core elements of a safety and health program:  
   *“Hazard identification and assessment”*  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

By routinely inspecting work processes, using the provided checklists to spot hazards, and controlling and monitoring those hazards, you create a systematic approach to keeping the workplace safe.



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 8)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)
2. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 7)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

results.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
results.answer:
**Cash method**

*  Income is put on the tax return **when it is actually received** (or constructively received, e.g., a bank deposit).  
   “Under the cash method, include in your gross income all items of income you actually or constructively receive during your tax year.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  
*  Expenses are deducted in the year they are **paid**.  
   “Under the cash method, you generally deduct expenses in the tax year in which you actually pay them.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)  

**Accrual method**

*  Income is reported in the year it is **earned** even if payment comes later.  
   “Under an accrual method, you generally report income in the year earned and deduct or capitalize expenses in the year incurred.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)  
*  Expenses are deducted (or capitalized) in the year they are **incurred**, regardless of when they are paid.  
   “Under an accrual method of accounting, you generally report income in the year earned and deduct or capitalize expenses in the year incurred.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)  

**Key difference**

The cash method matches income and expenses to the year they are actually received or paid, while the accrual method matches them to the year the economic event occurs—when you earn the revenue or incur the expense. This matching principle gives the accrual method a clearer picture of a business’s true financial performance for a given year.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)
3. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

results.question: can i deduct business travel
results.answer:
Yes.  According to IRS Publication 334 (Tax Guide for Small Businesses) you may deduct the ordinary and necessary costs of traveling away from home for business.  The guide makes it clear that those costs include:

* **Transportation** – the cost of air, train, bus, or car travel between your home and the business destination, plus fares for taxis, commuter bus, or limousine to and from the airport or hotel, and the cost of sending baggage or display material between regular and temporary work locations.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)  
* **Meals and lodging** – the expenses for meals and lodging on an overnight or otherwise long‑enough trip that requires sleep or rest.  You may use actual expenses or a standard meal allowance, and you can deduct only 50 % of meal costs.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  
* **Cleaning** – the cost of dry cleaning or laundry while on the trip.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  
* **Telephone** – business calls, fax, or other communication expenses incurred while traveling.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  
* **Tips** – tips paid on any of the above services.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

To qualify, the trip must meet the “away‑from‑home” criteria:  
1. Your duties require you to be away from the general area of your tax home for longer than an ordinary day’s work, **and**  
2. You need to get sleep or rest to perform your duties.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)

Only expenses that are ordinary, necessary, and directly related to your business are deductible.  No deduction is allowed for personal commuting costs (e.g., driving from your home to your regular workplace).  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35)



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 40)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 41)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

results.question: what goes in an executive summary
results.answer:
A business plan’s executive summary should be a short, concise overview that covers the key points of the plan.  According to the SBA Business Planning Guide it should:

> Executive Summary:  
> This portion should be brief; usually one or two paragraphs, but it should give the reader an overview of what you want to accomplish. For example, describe your idea, how much money you need, what you need it for, how much money you will bring (or have put) into the business, and a brief schedule of your goals. Since you won’t know some of these facts until you complete your business plan, write this section last.  

[cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)]



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 4)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

results.question: how do i describe my target market
results.answer:
To describe your target market, follow the guidance in the SBA Business Planning Guide:

1. **Identify the market niche** – state who your best customer is.  
2. **Describe that customer’s characteristics**.  
   - For business markets: segment by industry, company size, location, or product use/application.  
   - For consumer markets: segment by demographics (age, gender), geographic location, economic status, lifestyle, product application, or benefits sought.  
   *“Describe your market niche; who is your best customer. Identify those customers and describe their characteristics. Business markets might be classified by industry, company size, location, or product use/application. Consumer (household) markets might be segmented by demographics, (age, gender), geographic location, economic status, lifestyle, product application or benefits sought.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

3. **Estimate market size and growth potential** – use population figures, sales tax data, industry information, etc.  
   *“Estimate the approximate size and growth potential of the target market(s) using population figures, sales tax info, industry information, etc. Estimate how much of the total market you will capture.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

4. **Show how you will reach that market** – include location, distribution, promotion, and pricing that are tailored to the identified segments.  
   *“How will your promotional activities (such as advertising, personal selling or publicity) be tailored to your target market? Include rate sheets, promotional material and time lines for your promotional campaign.”* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=15)

Using these steps, craft a concise paragraph (or set of bullet points) that clearly states who your ideal customer is, the key traits that differentiate them, the size of that group, and the strategies you will use to capture a share of it.



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)
2. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=15)

results.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
results.answer:
You do need to make your shop physically accessible.  
The ADA Small‑Business Guide states:

- “When a business has two public entrances, in most cases **only one must be accessible**” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10).  
- If only one entrance is accessible, a **sign must direct customers to that entrance** and it must remain open during store hours [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10).  
- For parking, the guide says: “**If parking is provided for the public, designated accessible parking spaces must be provided, if doing so is readily achievable**” and that these spaces must be “closest to the accessible entrance and on an accessible route” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8).  

So, if your shop has two entrances you must make at least one of them wheelchair‑accessible and provide the required signage and access. If your shop has only one entrance, you still must remove barriers (steps, narrow doors, etc.) to make that entrance accessible whenever that is readily achievable. Additionally, if you offer parking, you must provide accessible spaces when doing so is readily achievable.



**Sources:**
1. [ada_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 10)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)
2. [ada_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 8)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)

results.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
results.answer:
You are only exempt from OSHA’s injury‑recordkeeping requirements if your business meets one of the following conditions:

* **You had 10 or fewer workers during all of the last calendar year,** or  
* **You operate in a low‑hazard industry specified in 29 CFR Part 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A.**

In either case you still must report work‑related fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye to OSHA, and you still need to keep the other mandatory reports if applicable. **[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)**

results.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
results.answer:
**Tax‑related records**

| What to keep | How long to keep it | Source |
|--------------|--------------------|--------|
| Records that support any item of income or deduction on a tax return (e.g., receipts, invoices, bank statements, canceled checks, payroll records) | Keep them **as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code**.  In practice that means keeping them **until the period of limitations for that return runs out**. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Copies of your filed tax returns | Keep them **for at least the same time you keep the supporting documents** (and often longer for reference). | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Employment‑tax records (including payroll, Form 941/944, wage and tax statements) | Keep them **at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later**. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| Asset‑related records (purchase price, depreciation schedules, sale documents) | Keep them **until the period of limitations expires for the year in which the asset is disposed of in a taxable disposition**. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |

**Injury & illness records (OSHA)**

| What to keep | How long to keep it | Source |
|--------------|--------------------|--------|
| OSHA Form 300 log, OSHA Form 301 incident reports, OSHA Form 300A annual summaries | Keep them **at the worksite for at least five (5) years**. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| Worker medical and exposure records | Keep them for the **time period required for each specific type of record** (e.g., medical records, chemical exposure logs). | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| OSHA‑required incident reports (fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, loss of an eye) | **Report them to OSHA within 8 hours** for fatalities, and within **24 hours** for in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, or loss of an eye. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |

> **Summary**  
> • For tax purposes, keep income‑related documentation until the IRS period of limitations expires (typically 3‑6 years, depending on the type of return), keep employment‑tax records for 4 years, and keep asset records until the limit period of the disposition year ends.  
> • For workplace injuries, maintain OSHA Forms 300, 301, 300A and related worker medical records on‑site for **5 years**, and provide OSHA the required fatality or severe‑injury reports promptly (within 8 hours or 24 hours as specified).

results.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
results.answer:
**To keep employees safe and keep your premises accessible, your small business should**

1. **Identify and control hazards**  
   * Conduct routine workplace self‑inspections to identify hazards, control them, and monitor the effectiveness of those controls.  
   * Use the self‑inspection checklists in the OSHA Small Business Safety & Health Handbook as a starting point.  
   * Example: “Workplace Self‑Inspection – an effective way to identify hazards … can help you identify hazards, control identified hazards, and monitor and evaluate hazard controls to verify that they continue to be effective” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8).

2. **Follow OSHA’s General Duty Clause**  
   * Employers must provide “a place of employment which are free from recognized hazards that are causing or are likely to cause death or serious physical harm to employees.”  
   * If a standard does not already address a hazard, the general duty clause applies.  
   * “Each employer – (1) shall furnish to each of his employees employment and a place of employment which are free from recognized hazards …” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91).

3. **Keep the premises physically accessible** (ADA Standards for Accessible Design, summarized in *ada_guide_small_business.pdf*)  
   * **Accessible parking** – provide designated accessible parking spaces that have an access aisle, clear vertical clearance, and the international symbol of accessibility.  If the parking lot has 25–50 spaces, provide 1 or 2 accessible spaces; if 1 space is provided it must be van‑accessible.  
     * “If your parking lot has 25 or fewer spaces, then 1 should be an accessible parking space. If it has 50 or fewer, it should have 2” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9).  
   * **Accessible routes** – all routes between parking, entrances, and key workplace areas must have no steps or steep slopes, and must have a firm, stable, slip‑resistant surface.  
     * “An accessible route must be provided between the access aisle and the accessible building entrance … it must have a firm, stable, slip‑resistant surface” [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8).  
   * **Entrances** – doors should be at least 36 inches wide (opening 32 inches); use lever or loop handles instead of knobs or round knobs that require a tight grasp.  
     * “Most entrances … use 36 inch wide doors … Changing or adding door hardware is usually relatively easy and inexpensive” [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12).  
   * **Ramps** – slope no steeper than 1:12, handrails on both sides if the rise is greater than 6 inches, and a clear landing of at least 36 inches by 90 inches.  
     * “When a ramp is added … the slope of the ramp should be as shallow as possible but not more than 1:12 … handrails whenever the slope is more that 1:20” [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10).  
   * **Signage** – install the international symbol of accessibility and, where required, “van accessible” or “accessible entrance” signs in visible positions.  
     * “A sign with the international symbol of accessibility must be located in front of the parking space … mounted high enough so it is not hidden” [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8).  
   * **Doors and turnstiles** – if a turnstile or narrow entrance is used, provide an accessible passage or gate that is at least 32 inches wide.  
     * “If an inaccessible turnstile is located for the entrance … a security gate or access passage must be provided … it must be at least 32 inches wide” [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13).  

4. **Employ training and communication**  
   * Use OSHA‑approved training programs (e.g., Outreach Training Program) to educate workers on safe work practices and the right to refuse unsafe work.  
     * “Employers must provide additional training for their workers on specific hazards of their job” [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=92).  

5. **Leverage compliance assistance**  
   * Take advantage of the OSHA On‑Site Consultation Program for free, confidential guidance on hazards and safety improvements.  
     * “The OSHA On‑Site Consultation Program offers no‑cost and confidential occupational safety and health services … to identify safety and health hazards in workplaces and how to fix them” [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90).  

**In short:** Scan the workplace for hazards, apply the OSHA general duty clause, keep parking and routes, doors, ramps, and signage ADA‑compliant, train employees, and use OSHA’s free consultation and training resources.

If you need clarification on any specific area—e.g., fire safety, slip‑resistance, or chemical hazard communication—please let me know and I can locate the exact passages that cover those topics.

results.question: how do i write a business plan and set up accounting
results.answer:
**Writing a Business Plan**

1. **Start with an outline** – a plan should include a cover page, an optional table of contents, an executive summary, a description of the business, a market analysis, an organization/management section, a description of products or services, an operations plan, a marketing plan, a financial section, and exhibits. The SBA guide says the outline is a good place to start:  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

2. **Cover page** – list the company name, address, phone number, owners, and the date.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

3. **Executive summary** – a short paragraph summarizing what you want to accomplish, how much money you need, how you will use it, and a brief schedule of goals.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

4. **Business description** – give an overview, industry background, why your business can compete, and future projections.  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)

5. **Products or services** – describe what you sell, why it matters, how it differs, and future offerings.  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)

6. **Market analysis** – identify your target market, size, and competition, and estimate how much of that market you will capture.  
   [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

7. **Organization and management** – state your legal structure, ownership percentages, board advisors, and detailed responsibilities for each key person.  
   [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13)

8. **Operations plan** – describe facilities, equipment, supply chain, inventory needs, and production capacity.  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)

9. **Marketing plan** – explain your product positioning, service level, and how customers will experience your business.  
   [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

10. **Financial section** – include historical financial statements (if any), a three‑year income projection, a cash‑flow projection, a balance sheet, a break‑even analysis, and a source‑uses of funds sheet.  
    [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)

11. **Exhibits** – add resumes, contracts, invoices, floor plans, etc., to support the content of your plan.  
    [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)


**Setting Up Accounting**

1. **Choose a tax year** – You can adopt a calendar‑tax year or a fiscal‑tax year (12 consecutive months ending on the last day of any month except December). If you start a sole‑prop business you must keep the calendar year unless you get IRS approval to change it.  
   [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

2. **Pick an accounting method** – the method (cash, accrual, special, or combination) must be used for all financial reporting. If you handle inventory, use the accrual method unless you qualify as a “small business taxpayer” that can treat inventories as non‑incidental supplies.  
   [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

3. **Keep complete, separate books for each business** – journal entries (receipts, expenses, payroll) and a ledger of totals.  
   [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

4. **Use a business checkbook** – open a separate business checking account, record expenses daily, and keep deposit slips, canceled checks, and receipts.  
   [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

5. **Reconcile monthly** – compare your bank statement with the checkbook and your books; correct any discrepancies.  
   [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

6. **Track supporting documents** – keep sales slips, invoices, deposit slips, and canceled checks to prove the amounts recorded in your books.  
   [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)

7. **Maintain electronic storage** – if you use an electronic system, it must provide indexing, preservation, and legible retrieval for the IRS.  
   [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

8. **Record petty‑cash** – maintain a petty cash fund for small payments; each use should have a slip and receipt.  
   [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)

By following the structure laid out in the SBA guide for your business plan and the IRS guidance for establishing a clear accounting system, you’ll create a solid foundation

results.question: what should i track for taxes and for travel expenses
results.answer:
**What to track for taxes**  

| What you need to keep | Why it matters | Where the document says it |
|-----------------------|----------------|---------------------------|
| **Gross receipts** – every dollar you receive from the business (e.g., sales receipts, bank deposits) | Needed to verify income on the return and to calculate net profit | *irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 11* – “You should keep supporting documents that show the amounts and sources of your gross receipts.” |
| **Expense receipts** – invoices, canceled checks, credit‑card slips, or bank statements for every business purchase | Supports every deduction you claim on your return | *irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 13* – “Proof of payment of an amount, by itself, does not establish that you are entitled to a tax deduction … you should also keep other documents, such as credit‑card sales slips and invoices, to show that you also incurred the cost.” |
| **Mileage log** – record of every business trip: date, purpose, starting & ending mileage | Required for claiming the standard mileage rate or actual vehicle expenses | *irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 40* – “You can deduct the cost of traveling ... by airplane, train, bus, or car … Car or truck. You can deduct the costs of operating and maintaining your vehicle … as actual expenses or the standard mileage rate.” |
| **Travel & lodging receipts** – hotel bills, airfare, train tickets | Needed so you can deduct 50 % of meals and 100 % of lodging, if the trip is overnight | *irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 41* – “Meals and lodging. You can deduct the cost of meals and lodging if your business trip is overnight … You can use actual expenses or the standard meal allowance … In most cases, you can deduct only 50 % of your meal expenses.” |
| **Business‑use portion of personal‑use items** – e.g., automobile fuel, parking fees, tolls, telephone, or internet used for the business | Allows you to split expenses between personal & business use | *irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 35* – “If you use your vehicle for both business and personal purposes, you must divide your expenses between business and personal use. … You can divide your expenses based on the miles driven for each purpose.” |
| **Tax‑specific records** – e‑actuals for excise taxes, employment taxes, and other taxes you file | Required for claiming those deductions and for IRS audit support | *irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 40* – “You can deduct on Schedule C (Form 1040) various federal, state, local, and foreign taxes directly attributable to your business.” |
| **Retention schedule** – the length of time to keep each type of record | Helps you know how long you must keep evidence and avoid penalties | *irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 16* – “You must keep the records as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision ... Generally, you must keep the records as long as they may be needed … until the period of limitations for that return runs out.” |

**What to track for travel expenses**  

| Item | What to log | Why it matters | Source |
|------|-------------|----------------|--------|
| **Trip date** | Date of departure & return | Establishes the tax‑year and whether the trip was “away from home” | *irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 40* – “You are traveling away from home if both the following conditions are met…” |
| **Destination** | City, state, or country | Required to show that the travel is for business | *irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 40* |
| **Purpose** | Meeting, conference, client site visit, etc. | Supports the “ordinary and necessary” test | *irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 40* |
| **Transportation method and cost** | Airfare, train fare, bus fare, rental‑car bill, mileage & rate | Needed to calculate the deduction for travel | *irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 41* – “Transportation. You can deduct the cost of travel by airplane, train, bus, or car …” |
| **Meal cost** | Itemized meal receipts | Supporting 50 % meal deduction | *irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 41* – “…you can deduct the cost of meals and lodging … in most cases you can deduct only 50% of your meal expenses.” |
| **Lodging cost** | Hotel bill | Supports lodging deduction | *irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 41* |
| **Parking & tolls** | Receipt or log | Deductible separately if using standard mileage rate | *irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 35* – “If you use your vehicle for both business and personal purposes … you can deduct business‑related parking fees and tolls.” |
| **Taxi / shuttle / limousine** | Itemized receipt | Deductible as transportation | *irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 41* |
| **Mileage log (if using mileage rate)** | Starting and ending odometer, business mileage | Needed to compute deduction and verify business use | *irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 35* – “Standard mileage rate ... 70 cents a mile (for 2025).” |

**How to keep the records**

1. **Attach receipts to a log or ledger** – keep each receipt next to the entry that shows the amount, date, and business purpose.  
2. **Separate personal & business expenses** – for mixed‑use items (e.g., a car or cell phone), keep a clear split of mileage or usage.  
3. **Maintain a dedicated file or digital folder** for each tax year so you can produce the records if the IRS asks.  
4. **Store electronic copies** – if kept electronically, ensure they are archived permanently in a format the IRS can read (e.g., PDF, scanned images).  
5. **Keep for the minimum required time** – at least 4 years for most business records, longer for assets or if the limitation period for a particular claim has expired.  

By tracking these items and keeping the documentation organized, you’ll be able to substantiate all deductions for taxes and travel expenses and comply with the IRS record‑keeping requirements.

results.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
results.answer:
You **do need an EIN** if your business:
- plans to pay wages to one or more employees, **or**  
- must file pension or excise‑tax returns.  
  (IRS Public 583, page 4)  

Even if you have no employees, most corporations, partnerships, and LLCs are required to obtain an EIN in order to file taxes and to keep proper records.  

The EIN itself does **not** determine which accounting method you use.  
When you file your first income‑tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040), you must **choose an accounting method**: either the cash method or the accrual method (or a special/combination method if needed).  
Choosing the method is independent of obtaining the EIN, although the EIN is required to identify your business on that return.  
(IRS Public 583, page 5; IRS Public 334, page 14)

results.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them
results.answer:
The OSHA small‑business handbook tells you exactly which injury records you must keep and for how long:

* **Forms you must keep**  
  – OSHA Form 300 (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses)  
  – OSHA Form 301 (Injury and Illness Incident Report) – a supplemental record for each recordable case  
  – OSHA Form 300A (Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) – an annual summary at the end of each calendar year  

* **Retention period**  
  “Injury and illness records (OSHA 300, 300A, and 301) are kept at the worksite for **at least five years**.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)
